subject: mathematics
question_text: If f: R − {0} → R is defined by f(x) = x + 1/x, prove that (f(x))² = f(x²) + f(1).

mark_split.label: Build the right side and match

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.9, chapter 2 FUNCTIONS, Very Short Answer question 6. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1 shape gives one mark to the expansion of (x + 1/x)² and one to building f(x²) + f(1), because the identity is exactly the statement that the middle term of the square equals f(1). Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1–Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — what you expand first, and what each piece on the right side works out to.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Expand (f(x))²
steps.margin_note: First mark is the expansion with the middle term present. The middle term 2·x·(1/x) is 2, and that 2 is the whole point of the question.
steps.memory_tip: (x + 1/x)² = x² + 1/x² + 2, because the middle term 2·x·(1/x) is always 2.

recall.must_convey: That (x + 1/x)² expands to x² + 1/x² + 2, with the middle term equal to 2.
accept: expand x plus one over x whole squared to get x squared plus one over x squared plus two
use a plus b whole squared and the middle term two x into one over x is two
the square gives three terms and the middle one is two
middle term two x into one by x equals two vasthundi
x square plus one by x square plus two is the left side
heard_as: x squared plus one over x squared

steps.why: The left side is the square of a two-term sum, so it opens with (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Here ab is x·(1/x) = 1, so the middle term is the plain number 2. Keeping that 2 visible is what makes the next step obvious.
common_mistakes: Writing (x + 1/x)² as x² + 1/x² and dropping the middle term.
Leaving the middle term as 2x/x instead of simplifying it to 2.
Using x = 0, which the domain R − {0} does not allow.

steps.label: Work out f(x²) and f(1)
steps.margin_note: Second mark is f(x²) and f(1) written out and matched to the first step. Check with x = 2: LHS = (2 + 1/2)² = 25/4, and RHS = (4 + 1/4) + 2 = 25/4.
steps.memory_tip: f(1) = 1 + 1/1 = 2, and 2 is the middle term of the square. That is why the identity holds.
lines: x ≠ 0 ⇒ x² ≠ 0, so f(x²) is defined.
LHS and RHS are the same expression.

recall.must_convey: That f(x²) = x² + 1/x² and f(1) = 2, whose sum is the expansion found on the left side.
accept: f of x squared is x squared plus one over x squared and f of one is two
add them and you get x squared plus one over x squared plus two which is the left side
put x squared into the rule and put one into the rule then add
f of one ante one plus one equals two
the right side matches the expansion so both sides are equal

steps.why: f(x²) is the same rule with x² in place of x, and f(1) is just the number 2. Their sum is exactly the expansion from the first step, so the two sides agree for every x in R − {0}. Squaring keeps x² away from 0, so f(x²) is always defined.
common_mistakes: Writing f(x²) as (f(x))², which is the left side again.
Substituting one number such as x = 2 and stopping; a single value is a check, not a proof.
